title: Apply 'best practice', mentoring, training and accountability in extension

lessons.title: Identifying and applying best practice
lessons.html:
What best practice means in extension

Best practice refers to methods and approaches that have been shown, through evidence and experience, to produce consistently good results in a given context. In extension it applies at two levels: technical best practice for farming, such as conservation agriculture, rotational grazing in camps or integrated pest management; and professional best practice for delivering extension, such as participatory planning, farmer field schools and systematic follow-up.

Best practice is context-specific

A practice that works for a commercial citrus grower in Limpopo may be unsuitable for a smallholder in the former Transkei with no irrigation and limited capital. Treat best practice as good practice proven in conditions similar to your clients', and adapt it carefully. Ask:

  • What evidence supports this practice, and from where?
  • Were the conditions similar in climate, soils, scale, resources and markets?
  • What would need to change for it to work here?
  • What are the risks if it fails?

Sources of best practice

  • Research institutions such as the Agricultural Research Council and universities.
  • Commodity organisations and their production guidelines.
  • Industry standards and certification schemes, such as food safety and good agricultural practice standards required by retail buyers.
  • Successful local farmers and documented case studies.
  • Professional extension bodies and peer networks.

Documenting and sharing practice

When a practice succeeds locally, document it: the situation, what was done, costs, results and lessons. Short case studies, photo records and farmer testimonies help spread good practice among colleagues and communities. Equally, record practices that failed and why, so others do not repeat mistakes.

Continuous improvement

Best practice evolves. Climate change, new varieties, pest resistance and market requirements mean today's recommendation may be outdated in a few years. Review recommendations regularly and keep up with in-service training and literature.

lessons.title: Mentoring and training farmers and colleagues
lessons.html:
Mentoring

Mentoring is a long-term developmental relationship in which an experienced person supports a less experienced person to grow in skill, confidence and judgement. In South African agriculture, mentoring is widely used to support new and emerging farmers, often by experienced commercial farmers, and to develop young extension officers.

Elements of an effective mentoring relationship

  • A written agreement covering goals, frequency of contact, duration, roles and confidentiality.
  • Goals set by the mentee with the mentor's guidance, such as achieving a target calving percentage or completing a first business plan.
  • Regular on-farm contact, not only telephone calls.
  • Building the mentee's own decision-making rather than making decisions for them.
  • Honest, respectful feedback and recognition of progress.
  • A planned end, when the mentee can operate independently.

Mentors must avoid conflicts of interest, such as using the mentoring relationship to buy the mentee's produce cheaply or to sell inputs.

Coaching and training

Coaching is shorter-term and focused on a specific skill. Training is structured learning for a group. Effective adult training follows principles of adult learning:

  1. Adults learn best when content solves their immediate problems.
  2. Build on learners' experience.
  3. Learn by doing, with practice and feedback.
  4. Respect learners as equals and involve them in planning.

Planning a training session

StepExample
Assess needsPoultry group losing chicks in winter
Set outcomesMembers can set up brooding correctly
Choose methodsShort talk, demonstration in a member's house, practice
DeliverHands-on session with local materials
Assess and follow upCheck brooders on visits, track mortality records

Where training forms part of a formal qualification, it must be delivered and assessed by accredited providers and registered assessors in line with the applicable quality council requirements.

lessons.title: Accountability in extension
lessons.html:
Being accountable

Accountability means taking responsibility for your actions and results, and being answerable to those you serve and those you report to. Extension practitioners are accountable in several directions:

  • Upward: to supervisors, the employing organisation and funders for plans, budgets and results.
  • Downward: to farmers and communities for the quality, honesty and relevance of advice and services.
  • Sideways: to colleagues and partners for agreed commitments.
  • Professional: to the standards and code of conduct of the extension profession.

Practical accountability tools

  • Personal work plans with clear targets linked to the organisation's operational plan.
  • Accurate records of visits, advice given, training and follow-up.
  • Regular, truthful reporting, including problems and failures.
  • Report-back meetings with farmer groups on programme progress and spending.
  • Client feedback mechanisms, such as feedback forms, farmer forums and complaint procedures.
  • Performance reviews based on evidence.

Accountability for advice

Advice can cause real losses if it is wrong. Give advice only within your competence, base it on reliable evidence, explain risks and uncertainties, and record what was advised. For regulated products such as agricultural remedies under Act 36 of 1947, always direct farmers to follow the registered label. Refer animal health questions involving medicines or controlled diseases to a veterinarian or the state veterinary service.

Ethics and integrity

Accountability depends on integrity: honesty, neutrality, confidentiality and fairness. Declare conflicts of interest, refuse gifts that may influence your recommendations, treat all clients equally regardless of background or political affiliation, and protect farmers' personal information in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act.

Learning from mistakes

When something goes wrong, admit it, inform those affected, correct it where possible and record the lesson. An accountable culture encourages open learning rather than hiding errors.

Key points

  • Best practice must be evidence-based and adapted to the local context.
  • Document and share both successful and failed practices.
  • Mentoring builds independence through agreed goals, regular contact and a planned end.
  • Training should follow adult learning principles and be followed up.
  • Be accountable upward, downward, sideways and professionally, with integrity.
